context: The excerpt identifies limitations and future directions primarily concerning perception, planning, human oversight, reliability, and safety. ORGANA currently uses independent sensor modalities, and the authors propose multimodal perception combining process parameters—such as temperature and stir rate—with visual cues including volume, color, and turbidity. They also note that robust, model-free perception of transparent objects remains unresolved because such objects can be textureless and reflective. ORGANA.PLANNER requires complex PDDL-domain definitions, which may be difficult for chemists without planning expertise; learning-based methods or LLMs could reduce planning time, although joint task-and-motion planning and scheduling currently add overhead. Human oversight remains important: users supported retaining humans in the autonomy loop, and half were uncertain about fully autonomous, start-to-finish operation. context: Zwirnmann et al. (2023) identify several manipulation limitations relevant to self-driving laboratory automation. Grasp robustness depends strongly on container geometry, grasp type, contact area, and gripper opening range. Some configurations have limited displacement tolerance when the container size is near the gripper’s minimum or maximum opening width, while low-height objects such as Petri dishes are difficult to stabilize in the x-direction. The most notable force-related weakness is the z-direction grasp of microcentrifuge tubes, where a force below 10 N indicates a need for optimization. The comparison with PaCoMe-like fingers also exposes a gripper-interface limitation: a planar interface can grasp only the loose lid of a Petri dish and therefore cannot lift the dish. Cutouts in the proposed fingers reduce contact area and can lower grasp force for some objects, although the authors regard this tradeoff as acceptable because stable transport, rather than maximum force, is the goal. The study’s future-oriented contribution is iterative design optimization through dual-extrusion 3D printing, varying fingertip geometry and soft materials. It does not address broader self-driving-lab issues such as autonomous error recovery, long-term reliability or uptime, calibration drift, throughput, safety certification, operating cost, or remote operation.

context: Burger et al. demonstrate an autonomous mobile laboratory workflow, while also revealing several practical limitations relevant to self-driving laboratories. Although the system could process up to six batches concurrently, this particular workflow used only two batches in parallel because preparation/reaction and analysis had similar timescales. Robot utilization was limited: it was charged but idle for approximately 32% of the experiment, primarily while waiting for the GC, identified as the slow step. The authors suggest that this idle time could be used for additional experiments in parallel, indicating throughput could be improved through faster analysis, greater parallelization, or better scheduling. Reliability depended on inventory monitoring and operator intervention: the system automatically alerted operators when vials or stock solutions were depleted and when workflow failures occurred. Most errors could be reset remotely, supported by continuous CCTV coverage, but this still implies that failures, consumables, and remote supervision remain operational constraints rather than being fully eliminated. It does provide a form of reproducibility and future extensibility by making station implementations, workflow software, and 3D labware designs available online. context: For Jiang et al. (2023), the dual-arm robotic dispensing platform is limited by material-specific failures and slower operation. Compressible powders can clog the spatula outlet, while hygroscopic or deliquescent materials can be difficult or impossible to dispense reliably; calcium carbonate and ammonium acetate, for example, had 100% failure rates in the reported trials. The platform is more versatile and precise for suitable solids, including abrasive and large-particle materials, but this comes at the expense of throughput because dispensing times are longer. The authors also note that the system cannot dispense sub-milligram quantities and may require alternative tools for larger particles or larger quantities. Precision for specific solids could be improved through manual calibration, although this reduces autonomy. Proposed future work includes self-learning dispensing algorithms tailored to particular solids, visual feedback to supplement analytical-balance feedback, and modular integration with mobile robots for vial delivery and transport. context: The excerpt provides limitations and operational considerations for the Zhou et al. 2025 LIRA system, particularly around calibration, localization reliability, and remote inspection. Eye-in-hand calibration uses multiple views of a stationary board to estimate the transformation between the robot tool and camera frames, allowing target poses to be converted into the robot base frame. Tactile calibration is described as slower because it requires sequential force-based movements and sensor validation. Vision-based ArUco calibration is faster and more flexible, but its reliability depends on image quality and can be degraded by lighting, reflections, and computational load. To improve marker-based localization, LIRA applies Gaussian filtering, subpixel corner refinement, and pose estimation; these steps address noise, motion blur, lighting variation, marker-edge jitter, and transient detection errors. (2022) demonstrate ARChemist through automated solubility-screening and crystallisation workflows using heterogeneous robotic platforms, but report several practical limitations. Solubility screening required an average of 12 minutes and was slower than a human-performed experiment, although it reduced repetitive work and enabled experiments to run for extended periods without continuous human attention. Reliability was imperfect: solubility screening succeeded in 9 of 10 runs, with one failure caused by the Quantos QS3 timing out during taring because of external vibrations. Crystallisation succeeded in 4 of 5 runs (80%); the failed run occurred when the Panda misplaced a vial while transferring it to the scale, highlighting manipulation and placement errors. The crystallisation workflow also took approximately 130 minutes on average. The paper presents the system’s configurable, loosely coupled architecture and intuitive chemical recipes as ways to support reconfiguration and automation, but does not provide a detailed error-recovery strategy, systematic calibration analysis, safety evaluation, cost analysis, or remote-operation study in this excerpt. Future work includes incorporating machine-learning advances for material discovery and moving toward multiple collaborative robotic scientists that can generate and test hypotheses with minimal researcher intervention.

context: The excerpt describes the vision-based closed-loop placement-error detection method, but it does not provide the specific measured accuracy, repeatability, overall placement-error distributions, success rates, or open-loop-versus-closed-loop comparison results requested. The geometric model (GM) estimates the transporter slot and transparent substrate boundaries using color masking, edge detection, Hough transforms, polygon aggregation, and convex-hull bounding rectangles. Detection is repeated over 100 camera frames, with appropriately sized bounds averaged before comparison. Using Shapely, the system evaluates area overlap and relative rotation; the GM classifies a placement as failed when overlap is below 90%. A failure triggers automatic removal of the misplaced substrate and replacement with a freshly dispensed one. The CNN component is trained for micro-scale rotational and translational errors using 1,990 original images, balanced between 996 failures and 994 successes, expanded through augmentation to 29,850 images. The excerpt states that GM and CNN performance is similar for rotational and translational errors, while performance differs substantially across small, medium, and large errors. It identifies small rotational errors as below approximately 1.7 degrees and large errors as above approximately 5.4 degrees, but gives no numerical accuracy or success-rate values here.

context: The excerpt reports vision detection and closed-loop correction performance for transparent substrate placement in a self-driving laboratory. Placement errors were categorized by magnitude: small rotational errors were below approximately 1.7°, large rotational errors above approximately 5.4°; small translational errors were below approximately 2.4 mm, while large errors exceeded approximately 5.6 mm. The fused geometric-model/convolutional-neural-network (GM-CNN) system detected all 20 large-error cases, all 12 medium-error cases, and all 4 small-error cases in the reported test matrix, with CNN confidence of 100% for large errors, 97–100% for medium errors, and 99–100% for small errors. The GM alone detected large errors effectively but produced false positives for medium and small errors. In ten pre-programmed placement failures, ASHE identified all ten failures and successfully corrected all ten on the second attempt. During 130 independent reload cycles without pre-programmed failures, 128 were classified as successful on the first attempt, giving 98.5% first-time placement accuracy; all 130 outcomes were validated by a human expert. The excerpt describes closed-loop performance but does not provide a quantitative open-loop versus closed-loop comparison, nor separate results for broader labware beyond transparent substrates.

context: The excerpt reports performance for ASHE, a closed-loop robotic system for manipulating transparent substrates in self-driving laboratories. In 130 independent substrate-reloading trials, it achieved 98.5% first-attempt placement accuracy, with only two misplacements. The remaining placements were classified as failures, automatically corrected through the reload protocol, and successfully placed on the second attempt, producing 100% correct placement by the second attempt. The fused geometric/deep-learning vision model classified small, medium, and large translational and rotational placement errors, with reported classification confidence between 97% and 100%. The system is described as accurate, reliable, repeatable, and capable of micro-scale error detection and correction, although the excerpt does not provide a separate numerical repeatability statistic such as variance, cycle-to-cycle deviation, or a confidence interval. It also does not report a direct open-loop versus closed-loop experimental comparison; instead, it emphasizes the benefit of closed-loop correction, particularly that false failure classifications are preferable because they trigger automatic reloading, whereas undetected misplaced substrates could cause downstream laboratory failures. The reported results concern transparent substrates rather than a broader set of labware. Generalizability is limited to the tested 50.8 mm × 76.2 mm × 1.0 mm glass substrates unless hardware is redesigned and the model retrained.

context: For MATTERIX, the excerpt identifies limitations primarily in chemical simulation and workflow verification rather than reporting quantified manipulation reliability, intervention rates, uptime, or remote-operation performance. The simulator supports only forward reactions expressible through SMARTS templates, and its reaction verification is explicitly semi-quantitative. The authors state that future improvements require more sophisticated, system-specific reaction-kinetics simulation and quantum-chemical calculations. For robotic manipulation, MATTERIX combines a skill library, differential inverse kinematics, cuRobo collision-free trajectory optimization, and reinforcement learning. The motion planner accounts for joint limits, velocity, acceleration, jerk, self-collision, and environmental collision avoidance. The authors report that commercially available grippers often lacked sufficient width to grasp microplates, so they fabricated custom fingers with a 3D printer. Their repeatability experiment found direction-dependent variation: the interquartile range was larger in the x direction than in the y direction, which they attributed to the orientation of the gripper fingers. In the lid-placement experiment, artificial positional offsets were introduced and success was assessed over repeated trials. Transfer success declined gradually as x-axis offset increased, while y-axis performance deteriorated sharply when the offset exceeded 2.190 mm. A transfer was classified as a failure when the lid rode up on the microplate and could not return to its starting position. These findings provide evidence of tight positional tolerances and sensitivity to gripper geometry/orientation, relevant to calibration and reliable manipulation. context: Seifrid et al. identify manipulation and motor-function limitations that are directly relevant to reliability, calibration, error recovery, and intervention rates in self-driving laboratories. Human-like dexterity and hand-eye coordination remain difficult to reproduce, particularly for troubleshooting and handling small quantities of solids. Automated solid dispensing is especially challenging for materials with different physical properties and for quantities below approximately 20 mg; achieving accuracy and precision requires extensive calibration and testing, which may be impractical when many solids need customized settings. The authors therefore describe a practical workaround: using stock solutions and established liquid-handling technologies to enable precise down-scaling. Heterogeneous mixtures also create risks for pump-based liquid transfer, including malfunction, blockages, and leaks, necessitating careful experimental design and continuous monitoring; solid-phase extraction may require human intervention. Some workflow operations, such as loading new vials or chemicals, still cannot be performed autonomously. Proposed future work includes robotic arms that imitate human actions, online computer-vision process control to monitor every operation and detect failures early, and redesigning experimental hardware to better suit automation and improve precision and reproducibility. In residual-sprue cutting, 190 specimens were processed across two experiments of 95 specimens each. There were two recoverable errors (1.05%): one picking failure and one incomplete cut detected and retried. Each experiment had one recoverable error. There were also two unsolved cutting errors (1.05% overall); Experiment 1 had zero and Experiment 2 had two. These failures were not detected by the verification algorithm, so the process continued and the defective parts required later disposal or possible human correction. After detected errors, one specimen was discarded to avoid desynchronizing injection and cutting. The authors programmed Telegram warnings for repeated picking failures, stopped injection, or persistent cutting problems, but state that these warnings were not needed in this example. Human involvement remained necessary for periodic material charging and changing, and the system is explicitly described as human-in-the-loop rather than fully autonomous. context: The excerpt identifies AgileX Piper as one of the commercial 6-DoF arms evaluated against OpenEAI-Arm and ARX R5. Under the same policy, dataset size, fine-tuning settings, and task suite, Piper achieved success rates of 0.86 for Clean Table, 0.40 for Make Tea, 0.80 for Fold Towel, and 0.50 for Fold T-shirt, giving an overall average of 0.64. The authors report that Piper’s failures were concentrated in grasp initiation and precise placement, attributing the performance gap primarily to its distinct kinematic and actuation design, which produces different local dexterity and control response and makes precise grasp alignment more difficult under the same fine-tuning budget. context: The excerpt describes a modular laboratory robotic platform designed to support both fully automated and remotely controlled chemistry and biology experiments. Remote users can operate the robot in real time through an online program, while webcams mounted on the robotic arm provide visual feedback for positioning and object localization. The platform is intended to interface with standard laboratory equipment and perform liquid handling, mixing, cell seeding, culturing, and genetic manipulation. The article frames these capabilities as improving efficiency, reproducibility, accuracy, and scientific progress relative to human-led experiments. However, the provided pages are introductory and do not report specific measured outcomes from remote users, such as task-completion rates, latency, experiment success rates, throughput, reproducibility statistics, or comparisons between remote and local operation. They also do not provide quantitative results for particular remote biological or chemical experiments. Thus, this excerpt establishes the platform’s remote-operation functions and claimed advantages, but evidence about experimentally measured performance would need to be obtained from later sections of the article.

context: This excerpt reports a comparison between manual laboratory procedures and an automated robotic arm for biological experiments, rather than directly documenting outcomes of remote users supervising or teleoperating the robot over the internet. The platform was evaluated for cell seeding, passaging, and lentiviral transduction. Reported measurements included the time required for these tasks, counted HaCaT cells after seeding, and the number of EGFP-positive cells after transduction. The excerpt states that the automated process produced a slightly higher number of infected cells than the manual process, with a statistically significant difference (p = 0.038). Successfully transfected HaCaT cells were also examined by confocal microscopy, with Figure 6E providing fluorescent images and a 100 μm scale bar. The methods emphasize reproducible robotic motion: world-coordinate values were obtained with Get_world_pos.py, and pipetting actions were executed through the modularized pipette_motion.py function. Thus, the passage provides measured biological and procedural outcomes for robotic automation, but it does not specify internet-based remote supervision, teleoperation, user locations, network latency, or other remote-experiment metrics.

context: The excerpt describes an internet-connected robotic platform that supports remote supervision and teleoperation of biological experiments. The robot arm’s position and end-tip orientation are controlled by a dedicated controller, with high-level trajectory planning reported to maintain a repetitive error of 0.02 mm. A server PC communicates with the robot controller through TCP/IP, enabling exchange of robot commands and image-processing information. A webcam and Python OpenCV detect ArUco markers for location data, while a Python Tkinter graphical user interface allows users to remotely access the server and control the robot. The platform was used for automated HaCaT cell-culture procedures, including handling culture vessels and performing a transduction workflow. The study recorded the time required for the transduction method and compared Cellbot’s performance with that of a trained human worker. However, this excerpt does not report the numerical results of that time comparison, nor does it provide measured biological outcomes such as transduction efficiency or EGFP-positive cell counts. It only states that EGFP-positive cells were counted using ImageJ and that images were collected from three culture-dish areas.
